I said that I listened to Major Strange a little while ago and when I heard him arguing about these prices I thought of the days when the grain exchange was really functioning, when following the last war we had a price of over $2.73 a bushel for our wheat at Fort William. One year later, if I remember correctly, the price had dropped to just above $1. That was between 1920 and 1921. What we are anxious about is that this does not happen again. As I have said before, the producer of foods is not interested in a high price now and a low price hereafter. If we try now to gouge from the world the last cent for our wheat and other Canadian products, the world will do exactly what it did after the high prices following the last war. The countries of the world will endeavour to bring about their own selfsufficiency; they will endeavour to free themselves from the prices that we have exacted, and then our position will be exactly the same as it was when prices fell to low levels following the period I have mentioned. I have here the average cash prices for wheat. In September, 1920, the price was $2.73^. One year later, in November, 1921, the average price had fallen to $1.10 a bushel.
The C.C.F. stands for what? A policy of marketing boards, a policy of intelligent price levels. We demand stable and adequate prices, set by negotiations for a' period of years, and varied by taking into consideration the cost of living and production from time to time. May I add that what I have just said is really a repetition of what the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Burton) said earlier in this 63260-21
debate when he was placing before the house substantially our point of view on agricultural matters. It seems to me that this is the intelligent policy for this house and the country to pursue at the present time.
May I repeat, to take advantage of shortages and of starvation now in order to obtain high prices, when incidentally wheat producers have very largely disposed of the last crop and of their reserves, would in my opinion be a suicidal policy benefiting no one. When supplies are adequate it would result in a similar disaster to that which occurred between 1920 and 1921. National planning, in which the stability of farm prices is the fundamental consideration, must be based not on speculation but upon the stability of purchasing power of the farming population.
In conclusion may I say that I believe it would be in the interests of this country and of our wheat producers in particular if we could establish under the leadership of the united nations organization a method by which we should be able to guarantee quantities and prices both to the producer and to the consumer, on a world-wide scale, and that Canada should take part in such an organization and indeed help promote it. If I may say so, the social and economic council of the united nations organization in some of its phraseology clearly visualized such a plan. When I was present at San Francisco and on the committee which established the social and economic council, this was both formally and informally discussed by the delegates.
What we need, in the words of Henry Wallace, is an ever-normal granary not only for our own country but for the whole world. There is no reason why a series of good crops should be regarded as a disaster. A series of good crops surely ought to be an inestimable blessing to this country and to the world. My mind goes back to the bible, to the story of Joseph; to the story of Pharaoh's dream of the fat kine and the lean ldne, the seven fat years and the seven lean years. Often in the old book you can find a parable or a story that is applicable even in these most modern days. Joseph planned in Egypt. Joseph built granaries in the seven fat years, and, as we are tpld in the bible, there was com in Egypt during the seven lean years. In my opinion that is what the world must do in future-plan so that there may be foodstuffs in the event of widespread disaster such as we have at the present time; and I am not thinking only of the disaster of war. We have been told authoritatively, and I saw this repeated in London, in the U.N.O. records I have read, that even in peace time two out of every three living human beings in the world
